steps.html:
A ghost ship full of cannibal rats, drifting towards Britain. It was on the front pages, it had a Facebook page, and almost none of it was true. This lesson is about how a story gets retold until it stops being one.

  • Follow a news story being retold in conversation
  • Report a story with the right verbs and distance
  • Watch a documentary about how a story goes viral
  • Write a formal opinion essay

steps.answer: The ship existed and was adrift; almost nothing else
steps.why: The Lyubov Orlova had genuinely broken loose. There was no proof of any rats, and rats are not cannibals.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: The speakers use apparently, supposedly, she claims, according to the article and from what it said.
steps.prompt: What are all of these doing?
options: Making the story sound more dramatic.
Marking the information as second-hand, so the speaker is not vouching for it.
Showing that the speaker does not believe any of it.
steps.answer: Marking the information as second-hand, so the speaker is not vouching for it.
steps.why: They are distance markers. You can pass a story on without taking responsibility for it — and the film shows what happens when nobody does.

steps.title: How to pass a story on without owning it
steps.html:
Recycled from Lessons 37 and 38, aimed now at retelling something you cannot verify.

English has a whole set of devices for saying this is what I was told rather than this is true. Using them is not weakness; leaving them out is how a rumour becomes a fact.

Adverbs: apparently, supposedly, allegedly, reportedly. They can go at the front, in the middle, or at the end: Apparently she was born in 1887 / It took him six days, supposedly.

Naming the source: according to the article, it said in the reviews, from what I read, the paper reported that. This is the strongest option, because the reader can check.

Reporting verbs that withhold agreement: claim, allege, suggest. Compare She says she was born in 1887 with She claims she was born in 1887 — the second reports the same words and declines to endorse them.

Modals of deduction: She must have lived through some interesting events. That must have slowed him down. These are your own inference, clearly marked as such.

The trap: according to is never used with yourself. According to me is wrong. Use in my view or I think.

steps.title: The same sentence, four distances
steps.html:
1. The information: a woman in Mexico is 127 years old.
  2. No distance at all: She is 127. You are now responsible for that.
  3. Adverb: She is 127, apparently. You heard it; you are not vouching for it.
  4. Withholding verb: She claims she is 127. You are reporting her words and declining to agree.
  5. Named source: According to the Irish Independent, she is 127. Strongest, because the reader can check it. The film shows what happens when a story travels through all four and comes out the other end with the distance markers stripped off.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.prompt: The film calls the process 'a vicious circle'. What does it mean?
options: Newspapers report a story, it is shared and exaggerated online, and then other newspapers report the online version.
Social media users are less intelligent than journalists.
steps.answer: Newspapers report a story, it is shared and exaggerated online, and then other newspapers report the online version.
steps.why: Each turn of the circle removes a distance marker, until he assumed there were rats has become cannibal rats heading for Britain.

steps.title: Write a formal opinion essay.
steps.sub: 180–220 words. Title: Social media has made news less reliable. Give the case for, the case against, and your own view.
steps.placeholder: Open with the claim you are going to examine.
steps.html:
• Open by stating the proposition and conceding the evidence for it.
  • Give the case for, with one figure and one named source.
  • Give the case against.
  • State your own view, clearly marked as yours.
  • Use <i>claim</i>, <i>argue</i>, <i>point out</i> and <i>report</i> rather than <i>say</i> throughout.

Useful language

  • It is frequently argued that … , and there is evidence for this.
  • According to one estimate, …
  • Supporters of this view claim that … ; critics point out that …
  • It is said that … , although this is rarely demonstrated.
  • The dominant factor, in my view, is …
  • On balance, I would argue that …
steps.modelHtml:
It is frequently argued that social media has made news less reliable, and the evidence for this is easy to find. The 'cannibal rats' story of 2013 began with a coastguard's assumption, acquired a salvage dealer's claim, and reached the front pages as established fact. At no point did anybody check.

Supporters of this view point out that social media sites produce no journalism themselves. They are, however, now the dominant way people encounter news: in the United States, around a third of Facebook users report getting most of their news there. The people sharing those stories are not journalists, and nothing obliges them to name a source.

Critics of the argument reply that the problem is older than the technology. Newspapers exaggerated long before anybody shared anything, and circulation figures suggest they had more readers when they did it.

In my view both are right, and the change is one of speed rather than kind. What social media removed was the day between hearing something and printing it. On balance, I would argue that the loss of that day matters more than any of the rest of it.
